lesson.title: Nature's Own Experiment: What Twin Studies Reveal About Genes and Behavior
lesson.summary: This section explains the logic behind twin studies, psychology's most direct way of estimating how much a trait is influenced by genes, and the assumptions and limitations that come with that logic.
lesson.body:
Twins offer psychologists something close to a natural experiment for studying heredity. Monozygotic twins, commonly called identical twins, develop from a single fertilized egg that splits in two, so they share essentially all of their genetic material. Dizygotic twins, commonly called fraternal twins, develop from two separate eggs fertilized by two separate sperm, so genetically they are no more similar than ordinary siblings, sharing about half their genes on average. This built in difference in genetic relatedness, while both types of twins are typically raised in the same family at the same time, gives researchers a way to isolate genetic influence.

The core logic works like this. If a trait is influenced by genetics, identical twins should resemble each other on that trait more closely than fraternal twins do, since identical twins share more genetic material. Researchers often measure this using a concordance rate, the percentage of twin pairs in which both twins share a trait or diagnosis when at least one twin has it. When concordance rates run noticeably higher for identical twins than for fraternal twins across many twin pairs, that gap is treated as evidence that genes contribute meaningfully to the trait in question. If concordance rates instead came out roughly equal for identical and fraternal pairs, that would point the other way, suggesting the trait owes much more to shared or individual environment than to genetic overlap.

An especially powerful variation on this design involves twins who were separated early in life and raised in different homes, sometimes without knowing of each other's existence until adulthood. Because these twin pairs share genes but not a rearing environment, any similarities that show up between them, whether in personality, interests, or cognitive ability, are harder to explain through shared upbringing and become stronger evidence for a genetic contribution.

Twin studies are not without limitations. One well known concern is the equal environments assumption, the assumption that identical and fraternal twins experience equally similar treatment from parents, teachers, and peers. In reality, identical twins, who look alike and are often dressed alike or enrolled in the same activities as children, are sometimes treated more similarly by the people around them than fraternal twins are, which means environment is not perfectly held constant between the two groups, complicating clean conclusions about genetic influence. Researchers have developed statistical adjustments to try to account for this imbalance, but it remains a real caveat rather than something the design eliminates entirely.

Twin studies connect directly back to the concept of heritability introduced in the previous section. They are, in fact, the primary method psychologists have used to generate heritability estimates for traits ranging from intelligence to personality to risk for certain mental health conditions, turning the abstract idea of heredity's influence into an actual measurable number.
